message.content:
{
  "decision": "APPLY",
  "workflow_yaml": "name: Rolling Release

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "frontend/**"

  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  Build:
    permissions: write-all
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    if: github.repository == 'GUI-for-Cores/GUI.for.SingBox'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Set up pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
        with:
          version: latest
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "latest"
          cache: "pnpm"
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: cd frontend && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Build Frontend
        run: cd frontend && pnpm build-only
      - name: Create a compressed file
        run: |
          git rev-parse --short HEAD | tr -d '\n' > frontend/dist/version.txt
          cd frontend
          mv dist rolling-release
          zip -r rolling-release.zip rolling-release
      - name: Generate Changelog
        run: |
          set +e
          LAST_COMMIT=$(curl -L https://github.com/GUI-for-Cores/GUI.for.SingBox/releases/download/rolling-release/version.txt)
          echo -e "## Change log\n\n> Update time: $(TZ='Asia/Shanghai' date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")\n" > changelog.md
          git log $LAST_COMMIT..HEAD --pretty=format:"* %s" >> changelog.md
          if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
            echo "No changes found since last commit." >> changelog.md
          fi
          set -e
      - name: Create Release and Upload Assets
        uses: svenstaro/upload-release-action@v2
        with:
          repo_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          file: ./{frontend/{rolling-release.zip,rolling-release/version.txt},changelog.md}
          file_glob: true
          tag: rolling-release
          release_name: rolling-release
          overwrite: true
          draft: false
          prerelease: true
          body: |
            Rolling release built by GitHub Actions.
            To use this version, please install the "Rolling Release Assistant" plugin and enable "Enable Rolling Release" within the app.
",
  "rationale": "The workflow currently has no job timeout, relying on the default 6-hour limit. Historical runs (5 recent successes) complete in 30-40 seconds. Adding a custom timeout of 5 minutes (well above observed maxima) bounds runaway executions and reduces wasted CI resources. This matches pattern P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT, which reports estimated VM time reductions of 12.9% (free) and 8.1% (paid), and is supported by a measured experiment (experiment:batch-interactive-three--fb8b16eb65a11508) showing 26.8% elapsed time savings on a similar Node.js workflow. The change preserves all build/test coverage and does not weaken permissions or add privileged actions.",
  "evidence_ids": ["experiment:batch-interactive-three--fb8b16eb65a11508", "pattern:P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT"]
}

The user wants me to propose a CI optimization for the given workflow based on the evidence provided. I need to analyze the workflow and the evidence to see if any optimization applies.

First, let's understand the workflow:
- Name: Rolling Release
- Triggers: push to main branch with changes in frontend/**, and workflow_dispatch
- Concurrency: cancels in-progress runs for same workflow/ref
- Single job "Build" with permissions: write-all
- Runs on ubuntu-latest
- Only runs if github.repository == 'GUI-for-Cores/GUI.for.SingBox'
- Steps:
  1. Checkout with fetch-depth: 0
  2. Set up pnpm (latest)
  3. Set up Node.js (latest) with pnpm cache, cache-dependency-path: frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml
  4. Install dependencies: cd frontend && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
  5. Build Frontend: cd frontend && pnpm build-only
  6. Create compressed file (version.txt, zip)
  7. Generate Changelog (curls last release version.txt, git log)
  8. Create Release and Upload Assets using svenstaro/upload-release-action@v2

Now, look at the evidence patterns. There are many patterns from literature. I need to see which ones are applicable and have evidence support.

The evidence includes experiment examples and pattern catalog. The experiment examples show measured CI workflow on fork for some patterns. For instance:
- P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT: experiment shows adding timeout-minutes: 5 to job, with 26.8% elapsed savings.
- P-LIT-DISTRIBUTED-CACHE: experiment shows adding pip cache for Python project.
- P-LIT-ENV-CACHE: synthetic scenario replay.

But the workflow is a Node.js/pnpm project. The patterns from literature include:
- P-LIT-GHA-CACHE: Cache dependency downloads (modest benefit)
- P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT: Bound jobs with custom timeout (estimated benefit 12.9% free, 8.1% paid)
- P-LIT-CANCEL-STALE: Already have concurrency cancel-in-progress, which is similar.
- P-LIT-CHANGE-FILTER: Already have paths filter on push.
- P-LIT-FAIL-FAST: Not applicable (no matrix).
- P-LIT-SKIP-WORKFLOW: Not applicable.
- P-LIT-FAIL-SCHEDULE: Not scheduled.
- P-LIT-IDLE-SCHEDULE: Not scheduled.
- P-LIT-FAILED-JOB-FIRST: Not applicable (single job).
- P-LIT-HISTORY-TIMEOUT: Could derive timeout from history.
- P-LIT-PRIORITIZE: Not applicable (no tests).
- P-LIT-BUILD-PRIORITY: Not applicable.
- P-LIT-SELECT: Not applicable.
- P-LIT-BUILD-SELECT: Not applicable.
- P-LIT-BAZEL-PARALLEL: Not Bazel.
- P-LIT-BAZEL-INCREMENTAL: Not Bazel.
- P-LIT-BAZEL-DEPS: Not Bazel.
- P-LIT-ENV-CACHE: Reuse validated build environments (but for Travis-to-Kotinos, not GitHub Actions).
- P-LIT-UNAFFECTED-STEPS: Skip steps using traced dependencies (but for Travis).
- P-LIT-SMELL-REPAIR: Repair evidenced configuration smells.
- P-LIT-DURATION-PREDICTION: Research only.
- P-LIT-UNUSED-OUTPUTS: Remove genuinely unused outputs.
- P-LIT-DISTRIBUTED-CACHE: Share cached build dependencies (guidance).
- P-LIT-CONFIG-REUSE: Reuse work across compatible configurations.
- P-LIT-UNUSED-DEP-SKIP: Evaluate skipping unused-dependency updates.

The workflow already uses pnpm cache via setup-node with cache: "pnpm" and cache-dependency-path. That's a form of dependency caching. The pattern P-LIT-GHA-CACHE is about caching dependency downloads. The workflow already does that. However, the pattern says "Choose dependency download state rather than unchecked build outputs". The workflow caches pnpm dependencies. That's good.

But there is no explicit timeout on the job. The pattern P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT suggests adding a custom timeout to bound jobs. The experiment example shows adding timeout-minutes: 5 to a job and getting 26.8% elapsed savings. However, that experiment was on a different workflow (Node.js with eslint, typecheck, etc.). The current workflow might have variable run times. We need to check if there's a history of run times. The repository context includes ci_history with 5 runs, all success, but no duration data. The runs have created_at and updated_at, we can compute duration: 
- Run 42545708093: created 2026-11-09T01:27:57Z, updated 2026-11-09T01:28:34Z => 37 seconds
- Run 42545682481: created 2026-11-09T01:27:38Z, updated 2026-11-09T01:28:10Z => 32 seconds
- Run 42545643233: created 2026-11-09T01:27:09Z, updated 2026-11-09T01:27:45Z => 36 seconds
- Run 42543785179: created 2026-11-09T01:06:47Z, updated 2026-11-09T01:07:20Z => 33 seconds
- Run 42058193542: created 2026-11-05T15:45:25Z, updated 2026-11-05T15:46:05Z => 40 seconds

All runs are around 30-40 seconds. So a timeout of 5 minutes (300 seconds) would be safe with huge headroom. The pattern P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT requires "Representative successful-duration history exists". We have 5 successful runs, all under 1 minute. So we can set a timeout of, say, 5 minutes (or 10 minutes) to prevent runaway jobs. The experiment example used 5 minutes. The pattern's reported result: vm_time_reduction_percent free 12.9%, paid 8.1%. That's estimated benefit.

But we must ensure we don't break valid slow runs. The contraindications: "Valid slow runs exceed the proposed limit". Since the longest observed is 40 seconds, 5 minutes is safe.

Also, the workflow has permissions: write-all. That's broad. Could we reduce permissions? The pattern P-LIT-SMELL-REPAIR might suggest fixing configuration smells like excessive permissions. But the evidence for that is secondary report only. The pattern P-LIT-SMELL-REPAIR is about repairing evidenced configuration smells. The example shows changing permissions? Not sure. The workflow uses write-all for the release action. The release action needs write permissions to create releases and upload assets. The svenstaro/upload-release-action requires repo_token with write permissions. So write-all might be necessary. But we could scope to contents: write, etc. However, the pattern P-LIT-SMELL-REPAIR is not strongly evidenced.

Another pattern: P-LIT-GHA-CACHE. The workflow already caches pnpm dependencies. But maybe we can also cache the node_modules? Actually, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile with cache: pnpm should cache the store. That's fine.

What about P-LIT-DISTRIBUTED-CACHE? That's about sharing cached build dependencies across runners, but it's guidance only.

The workflow does not have any matrix, so fail-fast not applicable.

The workflow already has concurrency cancel-in-progress, which is similar to P-LIT-CANCEL-STALE.

The workflow has path filtering on push (frontend/**) which is P-LIT-CHANGE-FILTER.

Thus, the only new optimization that seems applicable and evidence-supported is adding a custom timeout (P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT). The experiment example (document_id: experiment:batch-interactive-three--fb8b16eb65a11508) shows a measured CI workflow on fork with 26.8% elapsed savings. That's a strong evidence. The pattern P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT is also in the pattern catalogue with estimated benefit.

We need to check preconditions: "Representative successful-duration history exists". We have 5 successful runs, all under 1 minute. That's representative.

Contraindications: "Valid slow runs exceed the proposed limit". We'll set a limit of 5 minutes (or maybe 10 minutes) which is far above observed max.

Thus, we can propose adding timeout-minutes: 5 to the job.

Also, note that the job currently has no timeout. The default is 6 hours. Adding a timeout of 5 minutes will prevent runaway jobs.

We must preserve the intended build and test coverage. This change does not affect coverage.

Now, we need to produce the updated workflow YAML with the timeout added.

The workflow YAML currently:

jobs:
  Build:
    permissions: write-all
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.repository == 'GUI-for-Cores/GUI.for.SingBox'
    steps: ...

We'll add timeout-minutes: 5 under runs-on.

Also, we should consider if there are any other optimizations. The pattern P-LIT-GHA-CACHE is already implemented. The pattern P-LIT-ENV-CACHE is about reusing validated build environments, but that's more for Docker images or VM snapshots, not applicable here.

The pattern P-LIT-UNUSED-OUTPUTS: The workflow creates a zip file and version.txt and changelog.md, all uploaded as release assets. They are used. So not unused.

Thus, the only change is adding timeout.

We must include the complete updated workflow in workflow_yaml.

We'll set decision: APPLY, workflow_yaml: the updated YAML, rationale: explanation, evidence_ids: ["experiment:batch-interactive-three--fb8b16eb65a11508", "pattern:P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT"] (both evidence IDs). The experiment example is evidence of measured savings. The pattern catalogue provides the pattern details.

We must ensure we use only supported evidence IDs. The experiment example has document_id "experiment:batch-interactive-three--fb8b16eb65a11508". The pattern catalogue has document_id "pattern:P-LIT-CUSTOM-TIMEOUT". Both are in the evidence list.

Now, produce the JSON.

We'll copy the original and add timeout-minutes: 5.
